## Welcome

This bootcamp is built around one real, historical dataset: monthly Great Britain road-safety statistics from 1969 to 1984, including whether the front-seatbelt law was in force. In the real world, this dataset is a natural starting point for studying the impact of Great Britain's January 1983 seatbelt law — a classic natural-experiment case in policy evaluation.

Over the next four sessions we're going to unpack this dataset piece by piece: starting with the basics of R, moving through descriptive statistics and hypothesis testing, into visualization, and finally into a range of modeling strategies. Along the way we'll use it as an opportunity to explore *different approaches* to analysis — without trying to land on the single best design for evaluating this specific policy. That's a genuinely hard question in its own right (we'll flag where the tricky parts are, rather than solve them), and getting it fully right isn't this bootcamp's job.

Compared to previous editions, this one spends a bit more time on *design* — what question are we actually asking, and what's the right way to test it — and a bit less on pure coding syntax. With AI increasingly able to write R code for you, the more durable skill is knowing what logic you want that code to implement, and why.

## R Markdown

This is an R Markdown document. Markdown is a simple formatting syntax for authoring HTML, PDF, and MS Word documents. For more details on using R Markdown see <http://rmarkdown.rstudio.com>.

When you click the **Knit** button a document will be generated that includes both content as well as the output of any embedded R code chunks within the document.

If your code takes too long to knit, you can set the chunk option cache = TRUE, but be careful if the chunks create datasets that you need further down the line. We should also "block" with the "#" sign all packages from being installed and loaded in the library

Note also that, sometimes different packages have functions of the same name. Select a function from a specific package like this: `base::unique()`

R is *case-sensitive*. This means that inflation is different from Inflation. You can include . or _ or numbers in an object name. But you cannot start an object name with a number. Hence inflation2023, inflation.2023, inflation_2023 are all fine, but 2023inflation will not work.

### Variable types & assignment *(syntax demo)*
```{r}
a_variable <- 1983 # in R, "<-" is the assignment operator that allow us to create r objects -- this happens to be the year the Great Britain seatbelt law came into force
# you can see that now the object "a_variable" has been saved in our global environment
class(a_variable)
is.numeric(a_variable)
is.character(a_variable)
# as.numeric() # convert variables - also as.factor(), as.character()
# in general R works with 4 types of data: numeric, character, logical, and factor types.
# some extra care when converting factors to numeric

a_sequence <- c(1,2,3) #c is for concatenate - creates vectors
class(a_sequence)
sum(a_sequence)
2*a_sequence
length(a_sequence) # length of the variable


abc <- c("a", "b", "c")
# Note that a vector can only hold elements of the same type. For example, you cannot have a vector that contains both characters and numeric values.
class(abc)
print(abc)

```

### Sequences & matrices *(syntax demo)*
```{r}
another_sequence <- seq(from = 0.5, to = 1.5, by = 0.5)
print(another_sequence)

third_sequence <- 1:3
print(third_sequence)

rep1 <- rep(1, times = 5)
print(rep1)

rep2 <- rep(c(1, 2, 3), times = 3)
print(rep2)

rep3 <- rep(c(1, 2, 3), each = 3)
print(rep3)

# Let's have an insight on how r thinks
matrix <- cbind(a_sequence, abc)
print(matrix)
print(matrix[2,2])
# How to I get "3"? and how do I get "a"?

matrix2 <- rbind(a_sequence, abc)
print(matrix2)
print(matrix2[2, 3])
# How do I get "a" now?
# If I get confused between rows and columns and I ask to R "print(matrix2[3,2])",
# I get an error message: Error in matrix2[3, 2] : subscript out of bounds

# There are other variable types e.g. matrices, factors, data frames, lists
```

### Importing data

`Seatbelts` is real historical data (Great Britain road-safety statistics, 1969-1984) — but it ships built into base R itself, as part of the `datasets` package that's always loaded. No download, no `install.packages()`, no data-licensing question: it's already there.

```{r}
data(Seatbelts) # built-in, no file needed
class(Seatbelts) # a multivariate time series -- not a data frame yet
str(Seatbelts)

# Convert it to a regular data frame, and add a date + month column so we can work with
# it the way we work with any other dataset
seatbelts_monthly <- as.data.frame(Seatbelts)
seatbelts_monthly$date <- seq(as.Date("1969-01-01"), by = "month", length.out = nrow(seatbelts_monthly))
seatbelts_monthly$month <- factor(months(seatbelts_monthly$date), levels = month.name)

# Some ways of inspecting the dataset
dim(seatbelts_monthly)
summary(seatbelts_monthly)
head(seatbelts_monthly) # give you the top 6 values or rows by default (always scroll down!)
tail(seatbelts_monthly)
str(seatbelts_monthly)
# generally the output of verbose functions (e.g. str) appear in the console, and the output of snappy functions (e.g. head) appears on the markdown

# law: 0 before the seatbelt law took effect (Jan 1983), 1 after
table(seatbelts_monthly$law)

# What if my data set had a different extension, let's say, it was created in Stata?
# install.packages("haven")
library(haven)
dir.create("../data", showWarnings = FALSE) # make sure the folder we're about to write into exists
write_dta(seatbelts_monthly, "../data/seatbelts_monthly_demo.dta") # write our own data out as .dta...
seatbelts_from_stata <- read_dta("../data/seatbelts_monthly_demo.dta") # ...and read it straight back in, just to see the mechanics
str(seatbelts_from_stata)
```

### Subsetting
```{r}
## (1) Basic R syntax
# Select the first 10 observations
seatbelts_10 <- seatbelts_monthly[1:10, ]
print(seatbelts_10)

# Select columns
seatbelts_cols <- seatbelts_monthly[, c("date", "DriversKilled", "law")]
print(head(seatbelts_cols))

# Using the "subset" function, subset by condition
seatbelts_postlaw <- subset(seatbelts_monthly, law == 1)
dim(seatbelts_postlaw) # only 23 months -- the law took effect in Jan 1983, and our data ends Dec 1984

## (2) dplyr syntax
install.packages("dplyr")
library(dplyr)

# Select columns
seatbelts_select <- select(seatbelts_monthly, date, DriversKilled, kms, law)

# Select rows
seatbelts_1980s <- filter(seatbelts_monthly, date >= as.Date("1980-01-01"))

# Chain operations -- and here's an important design decision, not just a coding one:
# comparing ALL 169 pre-law months against the 23 post-law months would mostly be
# comparing two very different eras (cars, roads and driving all got safer over 15
# years, law or no law) -- not the law's effect. Narrowing the pre-law window keeps
# the comparison closer to apples-to-apples. We'll use this same window for the rest
# of the bootcamp whenever we compare before/after the law.
seatbelts_window <- seatbelts_monthly %>%
  filter(date >= as.Date("1980-01-01")) %>%
  select(date, DriversKilled, kms, PetrolPrice, law)
table(seatbelts_window$law)
# can you produce a narrower window, say 2 years either side of the law change instead of
# our 3-years-before choice? how many observations in each group do you get, and does the
# comparison feel any more or less trustworthy to you?
```

### Rename variables *(syntax demo)*
```{r}
# before renaming variables, I want to introduce you to the "$"
# in R, we can use $ to specify in which object R should look for something, e.g. in which data frame a certain vector (or variable) is stored
seatbelts_monthly_original <- seatbelts_monthly # keep an untouched copy so the alternative renaming methods below don't clash with the $ columns

seatbelts_monthly$deaths <- seatbelts_monthly$DriversKilled
seatbelts_monthly$distance_km <- seatbelts_monthly$kms
names(seatbelts_monthly) # we can check what really happened using the "names" function

# using function base R, starting again from the untouched original
seatbelts_base <- seatbelts_monthly_original
names(seatbelts_base)[names(seatbelts_base) == "DriversKilled"] <- "deaths"
names(seatbelts_base)[names(seatbelts_base) == "kms"] <- "distance_km"

print(head(seatbelts_base)) #see that in fact PetrolPrice did not change

# Renaming variables with dplyr, also starting again from the untouched original
# when we stop using basic R syntax and move to dplyr syntax, the pipeline %>% tells R where to look for certain info
seatbelts_renamed <- seatbelts_monthly_original %>%
  rename(
    deaths = DriversKilled,
    distance_km = kms
  )

print(head(seatbelts_renamed))

# we can also install the the plyr package and use the "rename" function... Let's try together
#install.packages("plyr")

```

### Omit NAs *(syntax demo)*
```{r}
# Seatbelts itself has no missing data, so for teaching purposes we'll pretend a handful of
# months' PetrolPrice reading went missing
set.seed(1)
seatbelts_monthly$PetrolPrice[sample(seq_len(nrow(seatbelts_monthly)), 5)] <- NA

is.na(seatbelts_monthly$PetrolPrice)
seatbelts_clean <- na.omit(seatbelts_monthly)
#how many observations did we lose?
dim(seatbelts_monthly) - dim(seatbelts_clean)

```

### Clean environment *(syntax demo)*
```{r}
rm(seatbelts_postlaw) # remove specific objects
rm(list = ls()) # to remove all objects - or just click the little broom
```
